1.1.explanation: Workflow versus agent is decided before the first line, because the wrong choice is the most expensive early mistake and the easiest to defend in a demo. Workflows fit enumerated steps, real error cost with step-level guardrails, standard observability, and well-constrained inputs; agents fit goals whose path cannot be written down, with non-determinism accepted and actions bounded by the toolset. The safe default is the cheapest pattern that survives your inputs: a single API call, then a workflow, then an agent.
1.1.example: A ticket router over five known categories is a workflow; an open-ended research task whose next step depends on what it just found needs an agent with a turn limit — and a workflow forced onto the research problem collapses on the first input that leaves the coded path.
1.1.guidance: Promote one tier only when the current one cannot absorb the input variety you actually see. The mismatch costs run both ways: a workflow where an agent was needed breaks off-path, and an agent where a workflow suffices buys nondeterminism you never use.

1.2.explanation: The agent is the pattern; the wiring path is an implementation choice. A loop calls tools, manages context, and runs until a goal is met, and three paths differ in who runs it: a raw loop over the Messages API (you own everything), the Agent SDK (the loop and scaffolding in your Python or TypeScript process), or Claude Managed Agents (Anthropic runs the loop and sandbox — but sessions are stateful and stored server-side, which rules them out for Zero Data Retention or HIPAA BAA workloads no matter how well they fit operationally). Set settingSources explicitly: it decides whether CLAUDE.md and Skills load.
1.2.example: A multi-hour monitoring task with no one owning the loop fits Managed Agents — unless a BAA constraint applies, in which case the Agent SDK in your own environment takes the same loop in-process.
1.2.guidance: Wire the loop identically on every path: register tools, scope the system prompt, return a tool_result for every tool_use with matching IDs — mismatched or missing IDs fail request validation and no prompt fixes that — and define explicit exit conditions, because a loop without them keeps requesting tools past what the task needs. Place the human checkpoint by worst-case cost: a loop that validated its edits in a scratch directory and then wrote to production is the characteristic accident.

1.3.explanation: Agent patterns compose tool-use loops with sub-agents, memory scopes, and context-window management, and frameworks such as Strands, LangGraph, and PydanticAI package the loop. Memory scope is a design-time choice among four: in-context (state in the conversation), external storage (a database read at session start), summarized memory (condensed history injected at start), and stateless (each session independent).
1.3.example: A cross-session assistant persists state to a database and reads it at session start, while a self-contained summarization job runs stateless and closes out — and a long dialogue injects a summary instead of full history.
1.3.guidance: Measure expected state size — history plus system prompt plus tool schemas — against the window before defaulting to in-context: too much inflates every call because the model re-reads the full history each turn, and tool outputs in production often run three to five times larger than test fixtures, so a window that held twenty turns in development fills at turn eight. Add a framework only when its abstraction earns more than the loop costs.

2.1.explanation: A business problem yields two kinds of requirement. Functional requirements name what the system must do, split across the model, existing systems, and people; infrastructure requirements name where it runs — which cloud, region, identity model, and compliance posture. The expensive failure is sketching the architecture mid-discovery: a stakeholder who sees a confident design assumes the questions were already asked, and the questions stop.
2.1.example: A document assistant's requirements name the extraction behavior and the model-versus-human split — plus a residency rule and an approval gate written down before design, because either would reshape the deployment if discovered later.
2.1.guidance: Write the constraint down when you hear it: an undocumented residency rule, retention rule, or approval gate becomes an infeasible system the moment production violates it. Requirements are captured, not inferred from a design.

2.2.explanation: A Claude application lives through the same lifecycle as any system — development, implementation, operation, maintenance — and the discipline is treating the prompt, the model pin, and the configuration as versioned, reviewed artifacts rather than live-editable conveniences. Knowing which phase an activity belongs to is what tells you when a phase can close.
2.2.example: A shipped assistant has a versioned prompt, a pinned model, and monitored error rates, so an iteration is a reviewed change with a rollback path instead of a live edit nobody can revert.
2.2.guidance: Exam items often mark the lifecycle phase and reject options that belong later, however sound they would be there — learn the phases as an ordering. Version everything that changes behavior, so a regression is a rollback rather than a hotfix.

2.3.explanation: Request shape follows who is waiting: synchronous for short responses and backend jobs, streaming when a user watches long output appear, the asynchronous client for concurrency without blocking, and the Message Batches API for bulk offline work within a 24-hour window at lower per-token cost. Streaming and batching never compete for one request — streaming changes perceived latency, batching changes the bill. Handling a stream safely is the scored skill: a tool_use block is SSE-chunked across delta events and is whole only after the stream closes.
2.3.example: A chat surface streams tokens as they generate; a nightly corpus-labeling job submits through Batches and compounds with prompt caching on the shared prefix. A dropped mid-tool-call stream is retried in full, never salvaged from the buffer.
2.3.guidance: Buffer stream deltas by index, rebuild the tool call from the finished block, and only then execute it — acting on a half-built block feeds malformed arguments downstream with no error signal. Every image and PDF consumes context before your prompt is read, so repeated images travel as URLs, and on the newest models sampling parameters such as temperature return a 400 — behavior is steered through prompting, confirmed against the API reference at build time.

2.4.explanation: The engineering substrate is ordinary production discipline: REST and JSON carry the contract, the SDK is a thin convenience layer over the same REST API handling authentication, request construction, retries, and parsing, and asynchronous programming keeps the application responsive while calls are in flight. Version control, code review, SDLC integration, and staged refactoring are scored as engineering discipline, not as Claude-specific trivia.
2.4.example: An integration keeps its Claude calls behind a reviewed service module with retries owned in one place, so a model or prompt change ships through the same review gate and rollback path as any other code.
2.4.guidance: Design the application to survive its own lifecycle — reviewed, tested, refactored in stages. Treat the SDK as a convenience over the wire contract, not a replacement for understanding it, because debugging starts at the contract when the abstraction misbehaves.

2.5.explanation: The same instruction is interpreted differently across Claude Code, Desktop, claude.ai, the API, and SDKs, so a prompt that works on one surface is a draft for another, not a finished artifact. Application design holds the content boundary — trusted instructions separated from untrusted content the agent fetches — keeps session hygiene by trimming or summarizing history before each call, designs schemas for the outputs the code consumes, and manages plugins as versioned dependencies rather than ad hoc copies.
2.5.example: A deployment prompt verified on the API is re-checked in Claude Code, where filesystem context and tool descriptions change what the model sees — and history is summarized before the window fills rather than after a failure.
2.5.guidance: The window is a ceiling, not a target: trim or summarize before each call, and keep fetched content marked as data. An unversioned plugin is an unaudited production change waiting for an upstream update.

2.6.explanation: Five configuration surfaces recur, and each is a governance choice: CLAUDE.md (project instructions loaded into every session, at the repo root), settings.json (permission mode, allow and deny rules, hooks — at user, project, local, and enterprise scopes), the model version pin (which snapshot the code calls, held by full model ID), prompt versioning (alongside the code), and plugin dependencies (versioned and tracked). Scopes resolve with deny winning over allow at any level, and enterprise managed settings cannot be overridden by users or projects.
2.6.example: A production app pins the full model ID instead of an alias, versions its prompts next to the code, and references its API key through an environment variable — so an upstream model update becomes a gated change and a leaked key is rotatable.
2.6.guidance: Pin the model snapshot, not the alias: an alias resolves to a moving target, and an upstream update becomes a silent production change with nothing to roll back to. The same discipline applies to prompts and plugins — version them with the code so a regression is a rollback.

3.1.explanation: Claude Code runs the agent loop in the terminal behind a permission layer that gates every action, working through tasks in explore, plan, and code phases, with plan mode holding it read-only until a plan is released. Its components each carry something different into a session — rules and CLAUDE.md for standing instructions, Skills for on-demand procedure, custom slash commands, subagents, and agent memory — and permission modes trade speed against oversight: default prompts before nearly every edit, acceptEdits auto-approves edits inside the working directory, plan mode proposes only, bypass silences everything including protected-path guards and belongs in an isolated container, and an allow-list mode auto-approves a named set while denying the rest for locked-down CI.
3.1.example: A refactor starts in plan mode so the proposed edits are reviewed before any write, switches to acceptEdits once the plan is trusted, and a deny rule on .env.production holds in every mode because deny wins over allow regardless.
3.1.guidance: Pick the mode from the worst-case cost of an unchecked action, and place settings at the right scope — user for the machine, project for everyone who clones, local for personal overrides that are git-ignored, enterprise for what cannot be overridden. Keep CLAUDE.md to the constraints that change behavior: it loads unconditionally into every session, so every line dilutes the one that catches a real mistake, and path-specific guidance belongs in rules files or Skills.

4.1.explanation: Every failure is first sorted as retriable or terminal, and on the Anthropic API the status code tells you: 429 (rate limit), 529 (overloaded), and 5xx server errors retry with exponential backoff, jitter, and honor retry-after; 400, 401, and 403 are terminal — the identical request fails again, so fix or reject the input. Tool errors come back to Claude explicitly with is_error true, and a refusal arrives as a 200 with a refusal stop reason — terminal, raised and logged, not retried.
4.1.example: A 429 from a burst backs off with a capped attempt count, while a 400 from a malformed tool argument raises immediately — retrying it would burn the retry budget and hide the bug behind identical failures.
4.1.guidance: Decide where retry lives: the SDK already retries transient failures with progressive delays, and wrapping your own loop around the same call multiplies attempts against the rate limit. Silence is what turns a tool bug into a plausible wrong answer — an empty result is never neutral. Use traces to localize the origin across four test levels, because most silent production breaks live at the integration handoff where each side passes its own tests.

5.1.explanation: Tokens are the unit of input, output, and cost — everything the model processes, including tool definitions and results, is counted and billed in tokens, and characters-per-token differs between model generations. The context window is the fixed budget everything shares, and two limits bite differently: an overflowing input fails validation before generation, while an input that fits can still halt mid-generation, returning what was produced so far under a context-window stop reason. Sampling makes generation non-deterministic — the same prompt can return different wording twice — so tests assert on properties that must hold, not exact text.
5.1.example: A test asserts the response parses and carries required fields in range rather than comparing an exact string that fails intermittently; in no case does the API quietly drop the oldest tokens — trimming history before each call is your code's job.
5.1.guidance: Think and budget in tokens, not words, and instrument usage per call from the start. On the newest models, non-default sampling parameters are rejected and behavior is steered through prompting — confirm current support at build time.

5.2.explanation: Technical fundamentals are the integration substrate: SDKs that wrap REST APIs, websockets as the streaming transport, and the ordinary disciplines any networked service needs — request construction, error handling, asynchronous execution so the application stays responsive while calls are in flight.
5.2.example: A service consumes the streaming API through the SDK's event interface while treating the REST contract as the source of truth for status codes and retry behavior.
5.2.guidance: Know what the SDK owns — authentication, request construction, retries, parsing — and what remains yours: timeouts, fallbacks, and where retry lives. Debug against the wire contract when the abstraction misbehaves.

5.3.explanation: Model choice and reasoning mode are two decisions set independently: which tier answers — Sonnet as the balanced production default, Haiku for speed and cost inside its envelope, Opus for demanding work above it — and whether it thinks before answering, steered by an effort setting rather than a token budget, with budget_tokens deprecated and erroring on the newest generations. Routing earns its keep only when request types differ: send the bulk to the balanced default and divert the few categories an eval shows need more or less.
5.3.example: A classification stage runs on a fast tier with thinking off, while a hard multi-step analysis pays for deliberation — and a proposed swap to a bigger tier ships only after the eval passes on your cases, because a model change is a release.
5.3.guidance: Start at Sonnet and move tiers on eval evidence in both directions, not merely to save cost. Respect the carry-back rule: thinking blocks return to the API verbatim on the next turn — their signature proves the reasoning was unaltered, and dropping one to save context fails the request. The exam is written against the three-tier blueprint framing, so treat any wider lineup as version-sensitive.

5.4.explanation: Cost management starts from three per-call metrics — token usage, latency, and error rate — instrumented from the start so a spike becomes a row you can sort instead of a mystery on the invoice. The levers are model selection, prompt and context size, call count, and streaming versus batch. Prompt caching reuses work on a stable exact prefix: the first request writes it, follow-ups matching up to the breakpoint read at a fraction of the cost, with a five-minute default lifetime refreshed on read and a one-hour lifetime at additional cost, applying only above a minimum token threshold.
5.4.example: A nightly labeling job batches its requests and caches the shared policy prefix, compounding both discounts — while a cache placed before a value that changes per request never hits, because ordering is the mechanism.
5.4.guidance: Model cost against the tail, not the average — token distributions are skewed and averages understate spend. Cache content that holds still: live state creates a consistency window, and a single changed character before the breakpoint invalidates the prefix.

6.1.explanation: Context engineering decides in advance what enters the window, what leaves as a summary, and what never enters at all. Four strategies each lose a different continuity: pruning rewinds and loses work after the rewind point, compaction loses whatever the summarizer did not capture, clearing loses all session context, and subagent handoff loses visibility into how the conclusion was reached. What compaction preserves depends on the summarizer — an under-specified one drops task-critical state such as which files were modified or which decision was taken at a branch point.
6.1.example: A multi-session agent's summarizer explicitly preserves modified files, the decision taken at each branch point, and resolved errors — because that lost state is one of the most common sources of multi-session failure.
6.1.guidance: Choose by the continuity you can afford to lose, and write the summarizer against the state the next turn needs. Subagent isolation keeps per-turn cost low and makes long-horizon tasks tractable, but a short workflow does not need the overhead.

6.2.explanation: Use the lightest prompting technique that clears the bar: instruction alone, then examples when showing the shape is easier than describing it — zero-shot for obvious shapes, one-shot to pin a structure a description keeps missing, multi-shot for specific structure, casing, or edge cases. Model capability and prompting mode are the same optimization: a stronger model clears zero-shot what a smaller one passes with examples, so run both down at once from the cheapest combination that satisfies the eval. Three failed revision passes is the cutoff for adding words — stop and ask which technique is absent.
6.2.example: A misshapen classifier output is fixed by two lines — an output constraint pinning the exact format and one few-shot example covering the ambiguous case — instead of a sixth round of longer prose that bloats the prompt for no accuracy gain.
6.2.guidance: The trap is a prompt that swells rather than sharpens: bloated prompts return bloated output and a latency hit. Sanitize inputs, place instructions at the right level (system versus user), and diagnose the missing technique instead of rewording.

6.3.explanation: Treat confident output with skepticism: a fluent response can be wrong with no error signal, so validate against the contract, parse defensively, and read stop_reason before treating any response as parseable — a refusal or a max_tokens cut returns non-matching text. When the format must hold, move it from the prompt into the API: passing a JSON schema enforces the grammar at generation time, in two forms — JSON outputs binding the final answer, and strict tool use validating arguments before your code runs them.
6.3.example: An extraction endpoint passes a schema so a shape-violating response cannot be emitted, and still checks stop_reason first, because the guaranteed schema does not guarantee success.
6.3.guidance: Structured output costs a slower first request per fresh schema while the grammar compiles, adds injected format tokens, and still says nothing about the value being right — validation confirms shape, and the eval guards the cases you did not think to test.

7.1.explanation: Prompt injection is the core threat for any agent that reads content it did not write: the hostile instruction rides inside fetched pages, documents, or tool results rather than the user's message, because the model flattens its entire context into one token stream with no native trusted/untrusted line. Jailbreaks and injections aim at different targets — the model's own guardrails versus your application's instructions — and one layered defense covers both: mark fetched content as data to inspect rather than instructions to obey, fence it with delimiters, and cap what the agent may do as a consequence.
7.1.example: An agent that fetches web pages treats page content as data, gates any consequential action regardless of what the page says, and passes PII only when the task requires it — guarding the prompt while leaving the action open is the common gap.
7.1.guidance: No agent that ingests untrusted content is fully immune; the application holds the boundary as well as the model. Least privilege bounds the blast radius: the same injection under a scoped identity is a denied action and a log line, under a privileged identity it is an incident.

7.2.explanation: Guardrails layer three questions, each at the point in the path where its harm occurs: input screening decides whether a request reaches the model, output screening whether a response reaches the user, and action authorization whether a side-effecting call may run — one filter at the far end covers exactly one of these and sits downstream of the only step that cannot be undone. Secure-by-design supplies the rest: least privilege, managed identity, and privacy shaped at design time. The failure direction is chosen deliberately, because a screening service that errors open is protection in appearance only.
7.2.example: Where an unscreened request would cause harm, the integration fails closed — if the screening layer is down, requests are rejected rather than passed through, and every privileged action writes an audit line.
7.2.guidance: A policy is not a control until the system enforces it and produces evidence. Choose check type by the question — classifiers for fuzzy intent, deterministic rules for formats and blocklists — and chain them knowing what each misses.

7.3.explanation: Hooks are enforcement, not convention: a PreToolUse hook runs before a tool call executes and can block it with a non-zero exit code, writing the reason to stderr the agent sees; a PostToolUse hook runs after, the right place for automated side effects and audit logging. Precedence when rules stack is deny over ask over allow — a single deny rule blocks the action regardless of how many allow rules are present, and an enterprise-level deny is the most durable control because no developer can remove it.
7.3.example: A destructive-write guard ships as a PreToolUse hook blocking writes outside the workspace with the reason on stderr, paired with a CLAUDE.md line stating the same intent — the instruction communicates, the hook enforces at every relevant call without exception.
7.3.guidance: Use both layers, because a rule in a prompt can be followed inconsistently and a hook cannot be skipped. In a regulated environment the audit trail from PostToolUse is the evidence that the control operated.

7.4.explanation: Secrets never travel with the configuration that references them: the config carries a variable reference and the value is injected at execution from an environment variable or a managed secret store, where one rotation reaches every consumer and every read is logged. A credential baked into committed code — a settings file, a source file, an MCP configuration — cannot be rotated, because overwriting the file never erases it from history. Identity is validated server-side, and the authorization configuration itself is a target: anything that can rewrite it acts with that identity.
7.4.example: An MCP server configuration references an environment variable for its token, the store rotates the token without touching any committed file, and production runs under an identity scoped to one output directory rather than one that can read every secret.
7.4.guidance: Scope every production identity to the narrowest access the task needs — the same injection under a scoped identity is a denied action and a log line, under a broad one it is an incident. Monitor authorized access, not just failed attempts, and protect the auth configuration as tightly as the secret.

8.1.explanation: Claude does not run your tools; it selects them and tells your code what to call — your code defines the schema, the model decides whether and when to call, your code executes and returns a tool_result, and the model continues, which makes the return path where most bugs live. Selection is driven almost entirely by the schema: the name, the description, and the input schema. Descriptions state what the tool does and when to use it, because vague or overlapping descriptions produce erratic routing, and every tool added costs tokens and dilutes the rest.
8.1.example: Two overlapping search tools cause erratic selection until their descriptions are rewritten to state distinct purposes and boundaries — routing stabilizes without any model change, and each tool_use is answered by a matching-ID tool_result.
8.1.guidance: Return tool errors explicitly with is_error so the model can change tack, ask, or halt — an empty result read as legitimate data is how a tool bug becomes a confident wrong answer. Audit the tool set like permissions: remove what the task does not need and record why removal was safe.

8.2.explanation: An MCP server packages a tool surface once so any MCP client can reach it, exposing tools, resources, and prompts over a transport — stdio for co-located processes, sockets for remote — chosen by where the server runs relative to the client. The payoff is reuse across clients; the cost is the extra layer, which only pays when more than one client actually exists.
8.2.example: An internal knowledge-base server written once is consumed by both a Claude Code deployment and a support agent — one place to fix, version, and authorize the surface, with its token referenced from the environment rather than committed.
8.2.guidance: Build an MCP server when reuse is real, and a direct integration when it is not — a shared protocol with exactly one client buys integration cost and no reuse. Keep credentials out of the server configuration, and version the server like any dependency.

8.3.explanation: Agentic customization chooses among four mechanisms per use case: built-in tools cover common capabilities with no configuration, custom tools bind Claude to your systems inside one application, Skills load task-specific procedure only when a request matches their description, and MCP shares one surface across many clients. Every mechanism costs tokens and selection accuracy, so the set the agent carries should be exactly the set the task needs.
8.3.example: A codebase task uses built-in file tools plus a project Skill for the team's release procedure, while a shared internal API is exposed once through MCP rather than re-implemented as a custom tool in every project.
8.3.guidance: Match the mechanism to the reuse pattern: a Skill for procedure that should load on demand, a custom tool for one application, MCP for a surface many clients share. Audit the combined set the way you audit permissions — capability the task does not need is attack surface as well as cost.
